title: Modelling association football scores
authors: Maher, M. J.
key_finding: Independent Poisson with team attack/defence parameters fits scores reasonably but shows small systematic deviations; a bivariate Poisson with score correlation about 0.2 improves fit.
relevance_to_system: Foundational caveat: even the originator of the independent-Poisson football model found residual dependence, so an uncorrected independent model misprices draws and correct-score-dependent lines such as Asian handicap.

title: Modelling Association Football Scores and Inefficiencies in the Football Betting Market
authors: Dixon, M. J.; Coles, S. G.
venue: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series C (Applied Statistics) 46(2):265-280
key_finding: Adds a low-score dependence correction (rho) and exponential time-decay weighting to Poisson; a strategy betting only when model probability exceeded odds-implied probability by a threshold showed positive return on 1995-96 odds.
relevance_to_system: Canonical evidence that 0-0, 1-0, 0-1 and 1-1 are mis-modelled by independence; the system's independent Poisson has no rho term so its remaining-goals distribution is biased exactly where under/AH lines are decided.

title: Analysis of sports data by using bivariate Poisson models
authors: Karlis, D.; Ntzoufras, I.
venue: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series D (The Statistician) 52(3):381-393
key_finding: Replacing independence with a bivariate Poisson (plus diagonal inflation) improves model fit and specifically the prediction of the number of draws.
relevance_to_system: Independent Poisson under-predicts draws; the system's 1X2 re-pricing and AH level-handicap pushes will be systematically mis-valued, creating phantom edge against a market that prices draws correctly.

title: A dynamic bivariate Poisson model for analysing and forecasting match results in the English Premier League
authors: Koopman, S. J.; Lit, R.
venue: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series A 178(1):167-186
key_finding: Time-varying attack/defence strengths in a bivariate Poisson state-space model over 9 EPL seasons produced a significant positive return over bookmaker odds in 2010-11 and 2011-12 out of sample.
relevance_to_system: Shows the bar for beating the market: dynamic strengths estimated from years of results plus explicit score dependence, not a static rate read off one bookmaker's current line.

title: A bivariate Weibull count model for forecasting association football scores
authors: Boshnakov, G.; Kharrat, T.; McHale, I. G.
key_finding: A Weibull inter-arrival-time count process with a copula fits scores better than Poisson and gives positive Kelly-strategy returns in both the 1X2 and over/under 2.5 markets.
relevance_to_system: Goal inter-arrival times are not exponential, so a constant-rate Poisson remaining-goals model is misspecified for in-play over/under pricing; Weibull-type hazards are the published alternative.

title: Prediction and Retrospective Analysis of Soccer Matches in a League
authors: Rue, H.; Salvesen, O.
venue: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series D (The Statistician) 49(3):399-418
key_finding: Bayesian dynamic generalised linear model with Brownian-motion team skills and MCMC inference, estimating all teams' time-varying strengths jointly for next-round prediction.
relevance_to_system: Team strength is a latent, slowly-varying state that must be estimated jointly across the league; a model anchored on a single live price has no such state and cannot know when the market is wrong.

title: Dynamic modelling and prediction of English Football League matches for betting
authors: Crowder, M.; Dixon, M.; Ledford, A.; Robinson, M.
venue: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series D (The Statistician) 51(2):157-168
key_finding: Models 92 English league teams over 1992-1997 with autoregressive latent strengths and proposes computationally cheap approximations suitable for a betting application.
relevance_to_system: Demonstrates that dynamic strength models were tractable for betting two decades ago; the system's absence of any team-strength prior is a design gap, not a computational necessity.

title: Ranking soccer teams on the basis of their current strength: A comparison of maximum likelihood approaches
authors: Ley, C.; Van de Wiele, T.; Van Eetvelde, H.
key_finding: Compared ten maximum-likelihood strength models; bivariate and independent Poisson with exponential time-decay weighting (half-period tuned by cross-validation) performed best for current-strength ranking.
relevance_to_system: Gives a tested recipe for pre-match strength priors (time-decayed Poisson) that could replace the system's market-only anchor and make model-vs-market disagreement meaningful.

title: Using ELO ratings for match result prediction in association football
authors: Hvattum, L. M.; Arntzen, H.
key_finding: Elo-based ordered logit beat six statistical benchmarks on 16,015 matches but did not beat bookmaker odds on either statistical or economic measures.
relevance_to_system: Even a well-tuned ratings model underperforms the market; a model that is weaker than Elo (single-price anchored Poisson) should be presumed to lose to the market rather than find edge against it.

title: Determining the level of ability of football teams by dynamic ratings based on the relative discrepancies in scores between adversaries
authors: Constantinou, A. C.; Fenton, N. E.
venue: Journal of Quantitative Analysis in Sports 9(1):37-50
key_finding: pi-ratings outperform Elo and showed profitability against market odds over five EPL seasons 2007/08-2011/12 even after the bookmaker margin.
relevance_to_system: A cheap, published rating feature that beats Elo; it is a natural input for the system's learned model and a far stronger prior than a flat market offset.

title: Bayesian hierarchical model for the prediction of football results
authors: Baio, G.; Blangiardo, M.
key_finding: Bayesian hierarchical Poisson on Serie A 1991-92 suffers overshrinkage of extreme teams; a mixture prior on team effects fixes it and improves fit.
relevance_to_system: Shrinkage/pooling choices change tail probabilities; the system's tiny logistic market-offset model has no hierarchy at all and will overfit league-specific noise.

title: A hybrid random forest to predict soccer matches in international tournaments
authors: Groll, A.; Ley, C.; Schauberger, G.; Van Eetvelde, H.
venue: Journal of Quantitative Analysis in Sports 15(4):271-287
key_finding: A random forest fed with Poisson-ranking strength estimates and covariates outperformed all competing methods including betting odds on the 64 matches of the 2018 World Cup held out for validation.
relevance_to_system: One of few peer-reviewed cases of beating odds, achieved by stacking a statistical strength model into ML; the system's ensemble has no comparable strength component.

title: Modelling soccer matches using bivariate discrete distributions with general dependence structure
authors: McHale, I.; Scarf, P.
key_finding: Archimedean copulas generate bivariate discrete score distributions allowing positive or negative dependence between home and away counts, fitted to English league data.
relevance_to_system: Dependence between the two teams' goal counts can be negative as well as positive; assuming zero is a structural error for any line that depends on the joint distribution (AH, correct score).

title: Bayesian modelling of football outcomes: using the Skellam's distribution for the goal difference
authors: Karlis, D.; Ntzoufras, I.
key_finding: Modelling the goal difference directly with the Skellam (Poisson-difference) distribution removes the need to specify the correlation between scores for 1X2 and handicap outcomes.
relevance_to_system: Offers a route to price Asian handicap without the fragile independence assumption: model the margin directly rather than two independent Poissons.

title: Forecasting football match results in national league competitions using score-driven time series models
authors: Koopman, S. J.; Lit, R.
key_finding: Score-driven dynamic models for a high-dimensional panel of weekly results: the pairwise-count model gives the most precise forecasts while the goal-difference model is most successful for betting; both beat benchmarks.
relevance_to_system: Confirms forecast accuracy and betting profitability are different objectives; the system should evaluate both and not infer edge from log-loss alone.

title: A birth process model for association football matches
authors: Dixon, M. J.; Robinson, M. E.
venue: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series D (The Statistician) 47(3):523-538
key_finding: Over 4,000 English matches show the goal-scoring rate rises over the course of a match and depends on the current score; goals are modelled as interacting birth processes.
relevance_to_system: Direct refutation of the system's constant-scoring-rate assumption: remaining goals are under-estimated late in matches and the score-state feedback (leading team slows, trailing team pushes) is ignored.

title: A random point process model for the score in sport matches
authors: Volf, P.
key_finding: Goals are modelled as two dependent random point processes with Cox-type intensities depending on time, current score and covariates, estimated from match data.
relevance_to_system: Provides the counting-process formalism for a time- and score-dependent intensity that the system would need instead of lambda times remaining-time fraction.

title: Joint modelling of goals and bookings in association football
authors: Titman, A. C.; Costain, D. A.; Ridall, P. G.; Gregory, K.
venue: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series A 178(3):659-683
key_finding: A multivariate counting-process model finds a red card raises the non-penalised team's goal rate and the home team's scoring rate falls once ahead; prospectively tested against live spread-betting prices.
relevance_to_system: Peer-reviewed in-play model that explicitly models red cards and score effects and was tested against live prices; the system's rate model ignores both, so its edge against in-play lines is spurious after events.

title: A Bayesian Approach to In-Game Win Probability in Soccer
authors: Robberechts, P.; Van Haaren, J.; Davis, J.
key_finding: Bayesian in-game W/D/L model using time-varying game-state features (score, time since last goal, performance stats) produces well-calibrated probabilities that account for soccer's low-scoring stochasticity.
relevance_to_system: Shows calibrated in-play probabilities require game-state features beyond score and clock; the system's two-input rate model cannot be calibrated across match states.

title: A Bayesian In-Play Prediction Model for Association Football Outcomes
authors: Zou, Q.; Song, K.; Shi, J.
key_finding: Relaxes constant team strength and uses in-match performance to calibrate strengths; improves total-goals and W/D/L prediction though not goal-difference prediction.
relevance_to_system: In-play information should update team strengths, not just the clock; the system updates only remaining time and score.

title: Around the goal: examining the effect of the first goal on the second goal in soccer using survival analysis methods
authors: Nevo, D.; Ritov, Y.
venue: Journal of Quantitative Analysis in Sports 9(2):165-177
key_finding: Cox model on 760 EPL matches: a first goal can expedite or impede the next depending on when it occurs, and the hazard of another goal increases as the game progresses.
relevance_to_system: Goal hazards are non-constant and history-dependent; a memoryless Poisson remaining-goals model is wrong in sign in some match states.

title: Down to Ten: Estimating the Effect of a Red Card in Soccer
authors: Ridder, G.; Cramer, J. S.; Hopstaken, P.
venue: Journal of the American Statistical Association 89(427):1124-1127
key_finding: Using a Poisson-process score model with conditional likelihood, estimates the expulsion effect independently of team strengths and shows a red card materially raises the opponent's scoring rate.
relevance_to_system: Red cards change the intensity parameters; the system has no state variable for player count so any post-card 'edge' versus the market is a model artefact.

title: Estimating the Effect of the Red Card in Soccer: When to Commit an Offense in Exchange for Preventing a Goal Opportunity
authors: Vecer, J.; Kopriva, F.; Ichiba, T.
venue: Journal of Quantitative Analysis in Sports 5(1), Article 8
key_finding: From in-play betting data on World Cup 2006 and Euro 2008, the penalised team's scoring intensity drops significantly while the opponent's rises slightly; total goals fall when a stronger team is penalised.
relevance_to_system: Uses in-play odds themselves to estimate intensity shifts, showing the market already embeds red-card effects that the system's model lacks.

title: Effects of a red card on goal-scoring in World Cup football matches
authors: Cerveny, J.; van Ours, J. C.; van Tuijl, M. A.
key_finding: Hazard-rate model over World Cups 1998-2014: the sanctioned team's goal-scoring rate falls and the non-sanctioned team's rate rises after a red card.
relevance_to_system: Independent replication of asymmetric red-card effects; any in-play model without a dismissal covariate is misspecified after the event.

title: Favoritism Under Social Pressure
authors: Garicano, L.; Palacios-Huerta, I.; Prendergast, C.
key_finding: Spanish referees systematically shorten close games when the home team is ahead and lengthen them when the home team is behind; injury time falls about 1.5 minutes per goal of home lead in close games.
relevance_to_system: Effective remaining time is endogenous to score and venue; using nominal remaining-time fraction mis-measures exposure for late in-play over/under and AH bets.

title: Temporal dynamics of goal scoring in soccer
authors: Ayana, G.; Ehlert, A.; Ehlert, J.; Santagata, L.; Torricelli, M.; Klein, B.
key_finding: Event data from 3,433 matches in 21 competitions show goal probability rises as matches progress, fewer-than-expected goals in the early minutes of each half, and bursty clustering of successive goals.
relevance_to_system: Recent large-sample confirmation that scoring intensity is increasing and bursty, contradicting the system's uniform-rate remaining-goals assumption.

title: Estimating the change in soccer's home advantage during the Covid-19 pandemic using bivariate Poisson regression
authors: Benz, L. S.; Lopez, M. J.
key_finding: Bivariate Poisson regression across leagues finds mixed changes in home advantage without crowds, decreasing in some leagues and possibly rising in others.
relevance_to_system: Home advantage is league- and period-specific and must be an estimated parameter; the system has no explicit home-advantage term beyond what the market line implies.

title: Home advantage in soccer: a retrospective analysis
authors: Pollard, R.
key_finding: Home teams obtained about 64% of all points in the English Football League, the largest home advantage among the major team sports examined.
relevance_to_system: Baseline magnitude of home advantage; any re-pricing of 1X2 or AH from a symmetric remaining-goals model must carry a venue effect.

title: A market-calibrated accelerated failure time model for in-play football forecasting
authors: Clegg, L.; Song, Z.; Cartlidge, J.
key_finding: A Weibull AFT goal-arrival model calibrated to Betfair kick-off 1X2 and over/under prices reaches 70.2% in-play accuracy versus 70.6% for Betfair on 140 EPL matches; market calibration is the main source of accuracy.
relevance_to_system: Closest published analogue to the system's design and it still only matches the exchange; it also shows pre-match market calibration, not the model structure, drives accuracy, so disagreement with the market is mostly model error.

title: Online bookmakers' odds as forecasts: The case of European soccer leagues
authors: Strumbelj, E.; Robnik Sikonja, M.
key_finding: On 10,699 matches from six leagues, bookmaker odds are effective probability forecasts, some bookmakers are better than others, and effectiveness increased over time.
relevance_to_system: Bookmaker odds are a strong, improving forecast; treating a single bookmaker's line as noise to be corrected by a simple model inverts the evidence.

title: On determining probability forecasts from betting odds
authors: Strumbelj, E.
key_finding: Probabilities derived with Shin's model are more accurate than basic normalisation or regression de-vigging; bookmakers differ as probability sources and the gap shrinks with market size.
relevance_to_system: How the system removes margin from the single bookmaker's line matters; naive normalisation biases the implied probabilities the whole model is anchored on.

title: Exploiting sports-betting market using machine learning
authors: Hubacek, O.; Sourek, G.; Zelezny, F.
key_finding: Training the model to reduce correlation with the bookmaker's implied probabilities (not just maximise accuracy) plus portfolio-style bet sizing yielded positive cumulative profit on NBA 2007-2014.
relevance_to_system: Edge comes from information orthogonal to the market; a model derived from the market's own line is maximally correlated with it and has no exploitable disagreement.

title: The Betting Odds Rating System: Using soccer forecasts to forecast soccer
authors: Wunderlich, F.; Memmert, D.
key_finding: An Elo-type rating updated from betting odds outperforms classic result-based Elo, and betting odds generally outperform mathematical models in forecasting soccer.
relevance_to_system: Market prices are best used as an input to ratings, not as a target to be out-predicted by a structurally weaker model.

title: Are betting returns a useful measure of accuracy in (sports) forecasting?
authors: Wunderlich, F.; Memmert, D.
key_finding: Theory, simulation and data from three sports show positive betting returns can arise systematically or randomly without superior accuracy; returns are a measure of profitability, not accuracy.
relevance_to_system: A short run of positive ROI in backtests is not evidence the model is right; the system must validate with proper scoring rules and out-of-sample calibration, not realised P&L.

title: PARX model for football match predictions
authors: Angelini, G.; De Angelis, L.
key_finding: Poisson autoregression with exogenous covariates for goals; the paper reports betting-strategy returns above 35% with a probability-threshold rule.
relevance_to_system: Illustrates how threshold-based 'bet when model disagrees with market' rules produce large reported returns that depend heavily on the threshold; such returns need deflation for selection.

title: Efficiency of online football betting markets
authors: Angelini, G.; De Angelis, L.
key_finding: Forecast-based efficiency test over 41 bookmakers, 11 leagues and 11 years: with best odds selected across bookmakers, eight leagues are efficient and three show exploitable inefficiency.
relevance_to_system: Inefficiencies are league-specific and require shopping best odds across many books; a single-bookmaker feed removes most of the documented edge.

title: Odds-setters as forecasters: The case of English football
authors: Forrest, D.; Goddard, J.; Simmons, R.
key_finding: Over 1998-2003 bookmaker odds' forecasting performance improved and matched or exceeded a statistical model, with the model unable to earn positive returns once odds information was incorporated.
relevance_to_system: Bookmakers incorporate statistical-model information; a model that is a function of the bookmaker's price adds nothing the price does not already contain.

title: Forecasting football results and the efficiency of fixed-odds betting
authors: Goddard, J.; Asimakopoulos, I.
key_finding: An ordered-probit results model finds weak-form inefficiency, with positive returns only for end-of-season matches under a high probability-gap threshold.
relevance_to_system: Edge, where it exists, is concentrated in specific contexts (season-end incentives); blanket in-play disagreement bets are not supported.

title: Combining historical data and bookmakers' odds in modelling football scores
authors: Egidi, L.; Pauli, F.; Torelli, N.
key_finding: A Bayesian hierarchical Poisson model that uses bookmaker odds as prior information alongside historical results improves predictive accuracy and calibration over either source alone.
relevance_to_system: The sound way to use odds is as a prior combined with independent data; the system uses odds as the only data source, so the posterior is the prior.

title: Information and Efficiency: Goal Arrival in Soccer Betting
authors: Croxson, K.; Reade, J. J.
key_finding: Using goals scored on the cusp of half-time as a clean identification, Betfair in-play prices update swiftly and fully to goal news with no drift.
relevance_to_system: In-play prices incorporate goals within seconds; a model that holds an anchored rate for up to 120 seconds after the line moves is stale, not informed.

title: The role of surprise: Understanding overreaction and underreaction to unanticipated events using in-play soccer betting market
authors: Choi, D.; Hui, S. K.
venue: Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization 107(B):614-629
key_finding: In-play bettors generally underreact to goals but overreact to highly surprising goals (underdog scores), with both statistical and economic support.
relevance_to_system: The documented in-play inefficiency is behavioural and event-conditional (surprise), not a steady-state rate mispricing; the system targets the wrong kind of disagreement.

title: Testing the Efficiency of Markets in the 2002 World Cup
authors: Gil, R.; Levitt, S. D.
key_finding: In-play prices respond strongly to goals but show some continued drift for 10-15 minutes afterwards, and bets on the pre-game favourite earned systematically negative returns.
relevance_to_system: Post-goal drift is the one documented in-play anomaly; exploiting it requires an event-driven strategy, not a constant-rate model, and favourite bias cuts against naive favourite backing.

title: Beating the bookies with their own numbers - and how the online sports betting market is rigged
authors: Kaunitz, L.; Zhong, S.; Kreiner, J.
key_finding: Betting when one bookmaker's odds deviate from the cross-bookmaker consensus produced positive paper and live returns, after which bookmakers restricted the authors' accounts.
relevance_to_system: Edge against a single bookmaker comes from the consensus of many books, and winning accounts get limited; a one-feed system has neither the signal nor a plan for limits.

title: Profiting from an inefficient association football gambling market: Prediction, risk and uncertainty using Bayesian networks
authors: Constantinou, A. C.; Fenton, N. E.; Neil, M.
key_finding: The pi-football Bayesian network combining ratings with subjective form, fatigue and motivation inputs showed profit against EPL 2010/11 odds and discusses risk and uncertainty of the betting decision.
relevance_to_system: Published profitable systems combine ratings with information not in the price and model decision risk explicitly; the system's offset model and fixed thresholds do neither.

title: A profitable model for predicting the over/under market in football
authors: Wheatcroft, E.
key_finding: Generalised Attacking Performance ratings built from shots and corners (not goals) forecast over/under 2.5 in ten leagues with an average profit of about 0.8% per bet over twelve years.
relevance_to_system: Shows the realistic size of over/under edge (under 1% per bet) and that it comes from shot-based information the market under-weights, not from re-pricing the market's own totals line.

title: Forecasting outcomes in tennis matches using within-match betting markets
authors: Easton, S.; Uylangco, K.
key_finding: Point-by-point in-play tennis odds correlate extremely closely with a structural match-probability model and anticipate service breaks up to four points ahead, indicating high in-play efficiency.
relevance_to_system: In-play markets track structural models almost exactly and even lead them; a structural model is a sanity check on prices, not a source of edge against them.

title: Incorporating domain knowledge in machine learning for soccer outcome prediction
authors: Berrar, D.; Lopes, P.; Dubitzky, W.
key_finding: The 2017 Soccer Prediction Challenge used 216,743 past results to probe the limits of predictability from results-only data; recency feature extraction and rating feature learning were the best-performing additions.
relevance_to_system: Results-only data has a hard predictability ceiling; a learned model trained on fewer, noisier in-play samples cannot be expected to exceed it.

title: Learning to predict soccer results from relational data with gradient boosted trees
authors: Hubacek, O.; Sourek, G.; Zelezny, F.
key_finding: Winning entry of the 2017 Soccer Prediction Challenge: gradient boosted trees on pi-ratings and PageRank-based team ratings outperformed relational learning approaches.
relevance_to_system: Tree ensembles on rating features are the proven ML baseline; a two-feature logistic market-offset is far below the state of the art.

title: Dolores: a model that predicts football match outcomes from all over the world
authors: Constantinou, A. C.
key_finding: Dynamic ratings combined with a hybrid Bayesian network trained on 52 leagues predicts matches in leagues absent from training, showing ratings transfer across competitions.
relevance_to_system: Cross-league transfer works through ratings, which argues for a pooled rating layer rather than per-league market offsets.

title: Predicting The Dutch Football Competition Using Public Data: A Machine Learning Approach
authors: Tax, N.; Joustra, Y.
venue: Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering 10(10):1-13 (preprint-format article)
key_finding: Public-data ML on the Eredivisie reached roughly 55% accuracy, about the same as a model using only betting odds as features.
relevance_to_system: Public-data ML roughly ties odds-only models; it does not beat them, so an ML arm must be judged against the odds baseline not against chance.

title: A deep learning framework for football match prediction
authors: Rahman, M. A.
key_finding: A deep neural network predicting W/D/L for the 2018 World Cup reports accuracy of about 63% on a small match sample.
relevance_to_system: Small-sample tournament accuracy claims carry wide confidence intervals; such results should not be read as evidence deep models beat market probabilities.

title: Machine learning for sports betting: Should model selection be based on accuracy or calibration?
authors: Walsh, C.; Joshi, A.
key_finding: Selecting models by calibration rather than accuracy produced higher betting returns, with a best case of +36.93% versus +5.56% for the accuracy-selected model.
relevance_to_system: Calibration is the decision-relevant metric for betting; the system's model and LLM arms should be selected and gated on calibration curves, not hit-rate.

title: Actions Speak Louder than Goals: Valuing Player Actions in Soccer
authors: Decroos, T.; Bransen, L.; Van Haaren, J.; Davis, J.
key_finding: VAEP values every on-ball action by its effect on the probability of scoring and conceding in the next actions, learned from event data.
relevance_to_system: Event-level state features (VAEP, xG) are the information in-play markets react to; a model fed only the price and clock lacks them.

title: A framework for the fine-grained evaluation of the instantaneous expected value of soccer possessions
authors: Fernandez, J.; Bornn, L.; Cervone, D.
key_finding: Expected possession value decomposes the instantaneous probability of scoring or conceding the next goal from tracking data into pass, drive and shot components.
relevance_to_system: The instantaneous goal hazard varies possession-by-possession; a constant per-minute rate is a coarse average that in-play markets with data feeds can out-price.

title: An examination of expected goals and shot efficiency in soccer
authors: Rathke, A.
venue: Journal of Human Sport and Exercise 12(Proc2):S514-S529
key_finding: Zone-based expected goals from 380 Premier League and 306 Bundesliga matches in 2012-13 quantify shot quality by pitch location and distance.
relevance_to_system: xG-type shot-quality features are a standard, cheap in-play signal absent from the system's inputs.

title: Machine Learning for Soccer Match Result Prediction
authors: Bunker, R.; Yeung, C.; Fujii, K.
key_finding: Survey finds gradient-boosted tree models such as CatBoost applied to soccer-specific rating features (including betting odds as ratings) perform best across the literature.
relevance_to_system: Confirms the field consensus: boosted trees on ratings and odds, not small logistic models or raw deep nets, are the baseline any ML arm must beat.

title: Evaluating soccer match prediction models: a deep learning approach and feature optimization for gradient-boosted trees
authors: Yeung, C.; Bunker, R.; Umemoto, R.; Fujii, K.
venue: Machine Learning (2023 Soccer Prediction Challenge special issue)
key_finding: For the 2023 Soccer Prediction Challenge the authors compare a deep model with feature-optimised gradient-boosted trees for exact-score and W/D/L probability prediction.
relevance_to_system: Most recent benchmark of DL versus boosted trees on soccer; useful reference point for any claim that the system's learned model is competitive.

title: Combining Machine Learning and Human Experts to Predict Match Outcomes in Football: A Baseline Model
authors: Beal, R.; Middleton, S. E.; Norman, T. J.; Ramchurn, S. D.
key_finding: Adding NLP features from journalist match previews to statistical features over six EPL seasons reached 63.18% accuracy, a 6.9 point gain over statistical methods alone.
relevance_to_system: Text-derived signals add value when combined with statistics in a disciplined model; an LLM arm should be evaluated as a feature source, not as a standalone forecaster.

title: The Deflated Sharpe Ratio: Correcting for Selection Bias, Backtest Overfitting, and Non-Normality
authors: Bailey, D. H.; Lopez de Prado, M.
key_finding: The Deflated Sharpe Ratio corrects a reported Sharpe for the number of trials, their variance, non-normal returns and track-record length to separate real findings from flukes.
relevance_to_system: Threshold and anchoring-window choices in the system amount to many trials; any backtest Sharpe must be deflated for them before being believed.

title: Backtesting
authors: Harvey, C. R.; Liu, Y.
key_finding: Provides a multiple-testing framework to haircut any reported backtest Sharpe ratio and a profit hurdle a strategy must clear to be deemed significant.
relevance_to_system: Gives the system a concrete procedure: count all strategy variants tried, haircut accordingly, and require the haircut Sharpe to clear the hurdle before deploying capital.

title: Solving the Problem of Inadequate Scoring Rules for Assessing Probabilistic Football Forecast Models
authors: Constantinou, A. C.; Fenton, N. E.
venue: Journal of Quantitative Analysis in Sports 8(1), Article 1
key_finding: Argues football W/D/L forecasts are ordinal and should be scored with the Ranked Probability Score rather than Brier or log loss, which ignore outcome ordering.
relevance_to_system: The system's evaluation should report RPS (and calibration) alongside log loss for 1X2 forecasts.

title: Evaluating probabilistic forecasts of football matches: the case against the ranked probability score
authors: Wheatcroft, E.
venue: Journal of Quantitative Analysis in Sports 17(4):273-287
key_finding: In experiments selecting forecasts for betting, the Ignorance (log) score outperformed both RPS and Brier, questioning the value of distance-sensitivity for this task.
relevance_to_system: Scoring-rule choice changes which model looks best; the audit should check that the system's model ranking is robust across log score, Brier and RPS.

title: Wisdom of the silicon crowd: LLM ensemble prediction capabilities rival human crowd accuracy
authors: Schoenegger, P.; Tuminauskaite, I.; Park, P. S.; Bastos, R. V. S.; Tetlock, P. E.
key_finding: Individual LLMs underperform human crowds, but an ensemble of 12 LLMs' probabilistic forecasts on tournament questions was statistically indistinguishable from the human crowd aggregate.
relevance_to_system: A single LLM arm is expected to be worse than crowd-type aggregates such as market prices; only large ensembles approach crowd accuracy.

title: Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
authors: Halawi, D.; Zhang, F.; Yueh-Han, C.; Steinhardt, J.
key_finding: A retrieval-augmented LM system with fine-tuned reasoning and aggregation nears the crowd aggregate of competitive forecasters on post-cutoff questions and surpasses it in some settings.
relevance_to_system: Near-crowd performance required retrieval, fine-tuning and aggregation of many samples; a prompted LLM making live bets has none of this machinery.

title: FIFA World Cup 2026 as a Contamination-Free Benchmark for LLM Forecasting Agents: Four Models, a Bookmaker, and 104 Matches
authors: Ding, J.; Guo, C.; Xu, J.
key_finding: Four frontier LLM agents forecast all 104 matches: none beat the bookmaker's Brier score, a flat stake on the market favourite out-earned every agent, agent ROI ranged from -18% to +10%, and betting against the market was unprofitable for all four.
relevance_to_system: Direct evidence that frontier LLMs do not beat bookmaker calibration on football and lose when betting against the market; the system's LLM arm should be treated as a non-edge.

title: WorldCupArena: Fine-Grained Evaluation of Language Models and Deep-Research Agents on Football Forecasting
authors: Wang, Z.; Gui, T.; Rao, J.; Di, S.; Tang, Y.; Liang, D.
key_finding: Against betting-market and human-fan baselines on the 2026 World Cup, the best LLM/deep-research system showed only small gains in result and exact-score accuracy, with a clearer gain only on a partial-credit scoreline metric.
relevance_to_system: Even deep-research agents only match market baselines on winner and score; no basis for an LLM arm to override market-implied probabilities.

title: LLM-SoccerArena: Benchmarking LLMs on Real-World Predictions in Sports
authors: Schroder, J.; Schweisthal, J.; Muller, O.; Weinmann, M.; Feuerriegel, S.
key_finding: A live forward-looking benchmark with seven LLMs on 104 World Cup matches finds web access improves Brier score by only 0.023 over no web access.
relevance_to_system: Giving an LLM live information yields marginal Brier gains; the LLM arm's value should be measured on logged, timestamped forecasts against the market, as this benchmark does.
